Pocket Pal, a Lab experiment

3DNew

A pocket game player with four games of its own and a reflective LCD you can see the pixels of.

Dependencies

three.jsRenderer, glTF + meshopt, OrbitControls Blender :: modeled, shadows bakedWeb Audio :: every sound synthesizedCloudflare Durable Object :: shared top ten

A screen with no backlight

Old handhelds had no backlight. You read them by the light in the room, every pixel threw a small shadow onto the layer behind it, and anything that moved left a ghost for a frame or two. I wanted that screen on a device that could sit on a desk today: a smoke shell you can half see into, the screen standing proud on its own slab, and a cartridge sticking out of the top.

The screen is 96 by 96

The games draw into a 96 by 96 grid of four shades, and the grid goes up as a texture once a frame. Everything that makes it read as an LCD happens in one fragment shader. Each cell is a square dot with a thin gap around it, then the same dot is drawn again, offset 0.22 of a cell, as a faint shadow underneath. That second lookup is most of the reflective look. The gap fades out once a cell drops below about three pixels on screen, otherwise a phone turns the grid into moiré.

The ghost happens before the shader. Instead of switching, each pixel eases toward its new shade by ghost^(dt·60), so at 0.72 a moving dot leaves a short smear and at 0 it leaves nothing. It’s on the Tune panel next to the shadow and the grid.

Four games, four rules

Each game borrows a genre and gets one rule of its own.

  • INK is a line that runs out. It loses a segment every 16 steps and each drop of ink gives back two, so you’re always racing your own tail.
  • SET drops three-cell pieces in three inks. Any full row scores 1. A row of one ink scores 5 and takes the row above with it, and chasing those is what stacks you high.
  • FOLD is a paper plane with no engine. Speed and height are the same thing, distance is the score, and flying low is faster and closer to everything that ends the run.
  • DOT bounces up a page that keeps rising. The third bounce on a ledge tears it, only a torn ledge scores, and every tear makes the page rise a little faster.

DOT changed the most. The first version paid you for every bounce, and playing it safe always won, so now nothing scores until something breaks.

The cartridge is the menu

Pick a game on the shelf and the cart on top lifts out of frame, the new one drops in, and the screen boots once it seats. The label is a canvas texture printed per game. The model’s UVs already belong to the shadow bake, so the label gets a second UV set at load, projected flat from its own bounds, and the print reads from that while the shadow keeps the first.

The cart is the one part I left out of the shadow bake. It was baked sitting in the slot, so every time it lifted out it carried a gray band of slot shadow with it.

The top ten

Every game keeps one shared board for everyone who plays it. Make the top ten and the game asks for three initials, arcade style: the d-pad picks the letters, 2 saves, and on a keyboard you can just type them. The title screen then cycles between the game’s logo and its board, with your own run marked.

The board can’t trust the browser, so it only checks that a score is possible. Every run is sent with how long it lasted, and a DOT run that tears ledges faster than the bounce allows never makes the board.

Looking at it

Orbit, Apart and X-ray sit next to Play. Orbit hands the camera to OrbitControls, with zoom held between 0.62 and 1.6 times the play distance and no panning, so the device can’t drift off the stage. Apart springs each layer off the body, glass first, 50ms apart, and everything still works while it’s open, so you can finish a game with the keys floating in front of the board. X-ray swaps every material except the screen for one fresnel shader in the page’s ink, and the LCD keeps playing inside the outline.

The moving parts

  • Lcd — the four-shade grid and its ghost pass. Draw with rect, text and sprite; it presents once a frame.
  • Deck — the console. The shelf, the cartridge swap and pause live here, so a game only implements reset, update, draw and playing.
  • KIT — every sound as data, two or three square, triangle or noise tones each, capped at 0.6s for effects and 1.6s for jingles, through a soft clip and a 280 to 3800 Hz band so it sounds like a small speaker.
  • EXPLODE — the Apart table, one line per layer: a name pattern, an offset and an order. Add a line to take another part off.
